mainTopic: End of פרק המפקיד (planning to misuse a פקדון, and the barrel cases) and the opening of פרק הזהב on which side of a coin exchange finalizes the deal
overview: The גמרא asks for the source of the dispute in the משנה about a שומר who only plans to misuse a פקדון. A ברייתא shows that בית שמאי learn from 'על כל דבר פשע' that a plan counts like an act. בית הלל require a real act, and read that פסוק as making him liable when he tells his slave or agent to misuse it. רבה limits the case of a tilted barrel: he pays only for what he took if the barrel broke, but if the wine soured he pays for all of it, since his own act caused that. שמואל says that lifting the barrel in order to take is already enough to make him liable. The גמרא explains this is because he wants the whole barrel as a base for his wine, not because a loss isn't needed. רב אשי asks whether lifting a purse to take one coin works the same way, and the question stays unresolved (תיקו). Then פרק המפקיד ends, and פרק הזהב opens with a משנה listing which side of a trade finalizes the deal: taking the item does, paying money does not. The גמרא begins with רבי changing his wording from 'silver acquires gold' to 'gold acquires silver' and starts to explain his reasoning, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Where do we learn this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the source of the משנה's dispute about intending to misuse a פקדון.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a פסוק behind the dispute in the משנה. This is a setup line; the answer comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, בית שמאי hold that a שומר who plans to misuse a פקדון is already liable, and בית הלל hold he is liable only after he actually misuses it. The גמרא wants to know which פסוקים each side relies on.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things known? (asking for a source)
An object left with someone for safekeeping
Misusing or taking for oneself an object one is guarding

phrases.english: Gemara: From where are these matters derived?
phrases.notes: He means the dispute in the משנה about someone who only plans to misuse the פקדון.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the dispute between בית שמאי and בית הלל about intent to misuse a פקדון

steps.title: בית שמאי: a thought makes him liable like an action
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings בית שמאי's source: 'על כל דבר פשע' teaches that planning counts like doing.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Rabbis taught: 'For every matter of trespass.' בית שמאי say: this teaches that one is liable for the thought just as for the action.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא and starts with בית שמאי's proof from the פסוק 'על כל דבר פשע'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית שמאי read the word 'דבר' (matter or word) as making him liable even for the plan of misuse. So for them, intending is already treated like the actual act.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter of wrongdoing or trespass
A thought counts like an action

phrases.english: As the Sages taught:
"For every matter of trespass"
Beit Shammai say:
This teaches that he is liable
for the thought just as for the action.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the source question with a ברייתא, starting with בית שמאי
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: בית שמאי learn from 'על כל דבר פשע' that a thought of misuse makes him liable like the act itself

steps.title: בית הלל: liable only after actually misusing it
steps.stepSummary: בית הלל say he is liable only once he actually misuses the object, based on 'אם לא שלח ידו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And בית הלל say: He is not liable until he actually misuses it, as it says: 'Whether he has not put his hand to his neighbor's goods.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives בית הלל's view and their פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית הלל point to a פסוק that speaks about actually 'sending a hand' into the object. For them, a plan alone does not create liability; only a real act does.

keyTerms.meaning: Until he actually puts his hand to it (misuses it)
His neighbor's goods or property

phrases.english: And Beit Hillel say:

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיִּשְׁלַח בּוֹ יָד,
phrases.english: He is not liable until he actually misappropriates it,
as it is stated:
"Whether he has not misappropriated his neighbor's goods."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to בית שמאי
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability comes only from an actual act of misuse, as the פסוק says 'שלח ידו'

steps.title: בית שמאי push back with their פסוק
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי challenge בית הלל: the Torah also says 'על כל דבר פשע'.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית שמאי said to בית הלל: But isn't it already stated, 'For every matter of trespass'?
steps.whatsHappening: בית שמאי challenge בית הלל: what do you do with our פסוק?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only an act creates liability, the words 'כל דבר פשע' seem to add nothing. בית שמאי argue that this פסוק must be teaching liability for the thought.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it already written?

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית שַׁמַּאי לְבֵית הִלֵּל:
phrases.english: Beit Shammai said to Beit Hillel:
But isn't it already stated:
"For every matter of trespass"!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית שַׁמַּאי לְבֵית הִלֵּל וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges בית הלל's position
steps.kashyaTarget: בית הלל's view that only an act creates liability
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק 'על כל דבר פשע' seems to make him liable even without an act, so בית הלל's reading leaves it unexplained

steps.title: בית הלל push back with their פסוק
steps.stepSummary: בית הלל answer back: the Torah also says 'אם לא שלח ידו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית הלל said to בית שמאי: But isn't it already stated, 'Whether he has not put his hand to his neighbor's goods'?
steps.whatsHappening: בית הלל turn the same kind of challenge back on בית שמאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a thought alone is enough, why does the Torah speak of 'sending a hand'? Each side now has a פסוק that the other side must explain.

keyTerms.meaning: He put out his hand (took or used it)

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית הִלֵּל לְבֵית שַׁמַּאי:
phrases.english: Beit Hillel said to Beit Shammai:
But isn't it already stated:
"Whether he has not misappropriated his neighbor's goods"!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית הִלֵּל לְבֵית שַׁמַּאי וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counter-challenge to בית שמאי
steps.kashyaTarget: בית שמאי's view that a thought is enough
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק describes an actual act of misuse, which suggests liability needs an act

steps.title: Then what does 'על כל דבר פשע' come to teach?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how בית הלל explain the פסוק 'על כל דבר פשע'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what does the פסוק 'For every matter of trespass' come to teach?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks: according to בית הלל, what is the purpose of בית שמאי's פסוק? This sets up בית הלל's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since בית הלל require an act, they still need some meaning for 'על כל דבר פשע'. The next step gives it.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the פסוק come to teach?

phrases.english: If so, what is the meaning when the verse states
"For every matter of trespass"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks בית הלל to explain the פסוק בית שמאי used
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What בית הלל learn from 'על כל דבר פשע'

steps.title: It teaches liability when he tells his slave or agent
steps.stepSummary: בית הלל explain: the פסוק teaches that he is liable even if he tells his slave or agent to misuse the object.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might think I only know that he is liable if he himself misused it. If he told his slave or his agent to do it, from where do we know? The פסוק says: 'For every matter of trespass.'
steps.whatsHappening: בית הלל give their meaning for 'על כל דבר פשע': it covers misuse done through his word, by a slave or agent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For בית הלל, 'דבר' means speech, not thought. So a שומר is liable when he instructs his עבד or שליח to misuse the פקדון, even though he did not touch it himself.

keyTerms.meaning: I would only know (this case)
His slave
His agent
From where do we know?

steps.whatToRemember: בית שמאי read 'דבר' as thought, so planning alone makes him liable. בית הלל require an actual act, and read 'דבר' as speech: he is liable if he tells his slave or agent to misuse it.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think בית הלל ignore 'על כל דבר פשע'. They use it too, but for a different case: misuse done by his word through someone else.

phrases.english: For one might have thought: I have only him himself,
phrases.notes: He means: I'd only know he's liable when he misuses it with his own hands.

phrases.english: if he said to his slave or to his agent, from where do we know?
The verse states: "For every matter of trespass."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'על כל דבר פשע' teaches liability when he tells his slave or agent to misuse the פקדון

steps.title: רבה: the tilted-barrel ruling applies only if it broke
steps.stepSummary: רבה limits the משנה: tilting the barrel makes him pay only for what he took if it broke, but if the wine went sour he pays for all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he tilted the barrel...' רבה said: They taught this only when it broke, but if it went sour, he pays for the whole barrel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the משנה, where he tilted the barrel and took some wine. רבה explains when its lighter ruling applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that if he only tilted the barrel and did not lift it, he pays only for what he took. רבה says this is when the barrel later broke. If opening it made the wine go sour, he must pay for the whole barrel.

keyTerms.meaning: He tilted the barrel
They only taught this in the case of...
It broke
It went sour

phrases.english: If he tilted the barrel, etc.
Rabba says:
They taught this only where it broke,
but if it fermented, he pays for all of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִטָּה אֶת הֶחָבִית כּוּ׳. אָמַר רַבָּה: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא נִשְׁבְּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: next clause of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Paying only for what he took applies when the barrel broke; if the wine soured, he pays for the whole barrel

steps.title: Why does he pay for the whole barrel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבה's ruling about soured wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why he should pay for all the soured wine when he took only a little. This sets up the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He did not lift the barrel, so he did not acquire it. The question is what makes him responsible for the whole barrel.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רבה's ruling
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why he pays for the entire barrel if the wine soured

steps.title: His own 'arrows' did the damage
steps.stepSummary: His own action caused the wine to sour, so he is responsible for all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was his own arrows that had an effect on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that opening the barrel is what made the wine go sour, so the damage comes straight from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the barrel breaks, that loss is not his act, so he pays only for what he took. When the wine sours, the damage comes directly from his opening it, so he pays for everything.

keyTerms.meaning: His own arrows (damage he directly caused)
Had an effect

phrases.english: His arrows
phrases.notes: A picture-phrase: like an arrow he shot, the damage comes straight from what he did.

phrases.english: are what had an effect on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His own act of opening the barrel caused the wine to sour, so he is directly responsible for the whole barrel

steps.title: שמואל: lifting with intent to take is enough
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that 'lifted and took' in the משנה doesn't require actually taking; lifting it in order to take already makes him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he lifted it and took from it...' שמואל said: 'took' does not mean he really took. Rather, once he lifted it in order to take, even though he did not take, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the משנה, where he lifted the barrel. שמואל explains what the word 'took' means there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might read the משנה as requiring two things, lifting and taking. שמואל says lifting the barrel with the plan to take is already enough to make him liable for the whole barrel, even before any wine is taken.

keyTerms.meaning: He lifted it
Actually, literally
In order to take
Even though

steps.whatToRemember: רבה: tilting only makes him pay for what he took when the barrel broke, but if the wine soured he pays for it all, since his own act caused it. שמואל: lifting the barrel in order to take makes him liable even before he takes anything.
steps.confusionAlert: The word 'ונטל' (and took) in the משנה is not a second requirement. Lifting with intent to take is enough.

phrases.english: If he lifted it and took from it, etc.
Shmuel says:
"Took" does not mean he actually took,
rather, once he lifted it in order to take,
even though he did not take.
phrases.notes: The גמרא leaves out the end: he is already liable for the barrel.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִגְבִּיהָהּ וְנָטַל הֵימֶנָּה כּוּ׳. אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לֹא נָטַל נָטַל מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: next clause of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lifting the barrel in order to take makes him liable even before he actually takes any wine

steps.title: Does שמואל hold that misusing an object needs no loss?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that שמואל's ruling shows he holds שליחות יד does not need any loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that שמואל holds that שליחות יד does not need a loss?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to learn a bigger rule from שמואל's ruling in Step 11. It suggests that, according to שמואל, a שומר can be guilty of שליחות יד even if nothing was taken away yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 11, שמואל said that just lifting the barrel in order to take wine makes the שומר liable, even before he takes any. Nothing is missing from the barrel yet. So it looks as if שמואל holds that שליחות יד does not need any חסרון (loss).

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It introduces a suggested idea, which is often rejected.
Misusing an object you are guarding, which makes the guard fully responsible for it
Loss: something actually taken away or reduced

phrases.english: Shall we say that Shmuel holds
that misappropriation does not require loss?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to draw a general rule from שמואל's ruling in Step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether שמואל's ruling shows that he holds שליחות יד does not need any loss.

steps.title: No, wine is different because the barrel keeps it fresh
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is rejected: the שומר wants the whole barrel to serve as the base for the small amount he wants, so it counts as if he took all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: No. It is different here, because he wants this whole barrel to serve as a base for that quarter-לוג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back. שמואל's ruling does not prove that no loss is needed. The wine case is special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small amount of wine keeps well only while it sits inside a full barrel. So the שומר who wants a רביעית actually wants the whole barrel to serve as its base. Lifting the barrel for that purpose counts as taking the whole barrel for himself. So שמואל's ruling does not prove anything about whether שליחות יד needs a חסרון.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different here: this case is special.
It is preferable for him; he wants it that way.
A base or support
A quarter-לוג, a small measure of liquid

phrases.english: They say: No,
it is different here,
since it is preferable for him
that this entire barrel will be
a base for that quarter-log.
phrases.notes: The small amount of wine stays good only inside the full barrel, so he really wants the whole barrel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in Step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that שמואל's ruling proves שליחות יד needs no loss.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The wine case is special: wanting part of the wine means wanting the whole barrel as its base, so it counts as taking all of it.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל did not say that a שומר is liable for just touching the object. The point is only that, with wine, his intent covers the whole barrel.

steps.title: רב אשי asks: lifting a purse to take one coin
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks whether lifting a purse to take one דינר also counts as taking the whole purse, as with the barrel of wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: If someone lifted a purse to take one דינר from it, what is the law? Maybe only wine needs the barrel to keep it, but a coin keeps fine by itself. Or maybe guarding a whole purse is different from guarding one loose coin?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי uses the reasoning of Step 13 and asks whether it also applies to coins in a purse. He lays out both sides of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side: wine spoils without the rest of the barrel, but a coin does not spoil. So taking one coin does not mean he wants the whole purse. Other side: one loose coin is easy to lose, while a purse is easier to keep track of. So he may want the whole purse to keep his coin safe, just like the barrel.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks a question that the גמרא does not yet know the answer to
A purse or money pouch
Is kept or preserved
Or perhaps. It introduces the other side of the question.
Guarding; how well something is kept safe

phrases.english: Rav Ashi raised a dilemma:
If one lifted a purse
to take a dinar from it, what is the law?
Is it wine that is not preserved
except by means of the rest of the wine,
but a coin is preserved even by itself?
Or perhaps guarding a purse is different
from guarding a single dinar?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the "base" reasoning of Step 13 and tests it on a new case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether lifting a purse to take one coin makes the שומר responsible for the whole purse.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי's question about the purse is left unanswered: תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends רב אשי's question without an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side is proven. The question of whether intending to take one coin covers the whole purse stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question stays unresolved.

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רב אשי's question from Step 14 with no answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is unresolved whether lifting a purse to take one דינר makes the שומר liable for the whole purse.
steps.whatToRemember: Lifting a barrel to take some wine counts as taking all of it, because the barrel keeps the wine fresh. Whether the same is true for coins in a purse is left as תיקו.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing פרק המפקיד
steps.stepSummary: The chapter המפקיד ends with the traditional closing line.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק המפקיד.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the chapter המפקיד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not part of the argument. It is the traditional farewell said when finishing a chapter, showing that we plan to come back and learn it again.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you: the closing words of a chapter
The name of the chapter now ending, about a person who deposits an object with a שומר

phrases.english: We will return to you, HaMafkid

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the whole chapter.

steps.title: New chapter: gold acquires silver, but silver does not acquire gold
steps.stepSummary: The new chapter's משנה teaches that in a gold-for-silver exchange, taking the gold acquires the silver, but taking the silver does not acquire the gold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Gold acquires silver, but silver does not acquire gold.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter, פרק הזהב, opens with a משנה about trading one kind of coin for another. It tells us which side's handover finalizes the deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Handing over money does not finalize a sale; taking the item itself does. When gold coins are traded for silver coins, silver counts as the "money" and gold counts as the "item." So when one side takes the gold, the deal is done and the silver is acquired. Taking the silver alone does not finalize anything.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין: our משנה
The gold. It is also the name of the new chapter.
Acquires; finalizes the purchase
The silver

phrases.english: MISHNA: The gold acquires the silver,
phrases.notes: Once one side takes the gold coins, the other side has acquired the silver coins. Gold is treated as the item being bought.

phrases.english: but the silver does not acquire the gold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new chapter on a new topic, buying and selling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a gold-for-silver exchange, taking the gold finalizes the deal, but taking the silver does not.
steps.confusionAlert: "Gold acquires silver" does not mean the gold buys the silver. It means that when the gold is taken, the silver is acquired, because silver plays the role of money here.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the chapter's main question: in any trade, which side counts as the money and which counts as the item. Only taking the item finalizes the deal.

steps.title: Copper and silver, bad coins and good coins
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues its list: taking copper acquires silver, but not the reverse. Taking bad coins acquires good coins, but not the reverse.
steps.simpleTranslation: Copper acquires silver, but silver does not acquire copper. Bad coins acquire good ones, but good coins do not acquire bad ones.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds two more pairs to the gold-and-silver rule from the last step. In each pair, taking one side finalizes the deal and taking the other side does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Next to copper, silver counts as the 'money' and copper as the 'merchandise.' Likewise, good coins count as money, and worn or rejected coins count as merchandise. Taking the merchandise side closes the deal, and the money side then belongs to the other person.

keyTerms.meaning: Copper (here, copper coins)
Acquires; finalizes ownership
Bad coins: worn out or not readily accepted
Good coins that are in full use

phrases.english: Copper acquires the silver,
phrases.notes: He means: once one side takes the copper, the other side now owns the silver.

phrases.english: but the silver does not acquire the copper.
Bad coins acquire the good ones,
but the good ones do not acquire the bad ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list that began with gold and silver.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In copper-for-silver and bad-coins-for-good-coins deals, taking the lesser item (copper, or the bad coins) finalizes the deal, but taking the better one does not.

steps.title: Unminted coins and goods compared to minted coins
steps.stepSummary: Taking an unminted coin (אסימון) acquires a minted coin, but not the reverse. Taking goods (מטלטלין) acquires a coin, but not the reverse.
steps.simpleTranslation: An unminted coin acquires a minted coin, but a minted coin does not acquire an unminted one. Movable goods acquire a coin, but a coin does not acquire movable goods.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives two more pairs, ending with the most basic one: goods versus money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אסימון is a metal blank with no official stamp, so it acts like merchandise next to a real coin. This leads to the clearest case: goods for money. Taking the goods finalizes the deal, but handing over the coin does not.

keyTerms.meaning: An unminted coin, a metal blank with no official stamp
A minted coin in use as money
Movable property; goods that can be carried

phrases.english: An unminted coin acquires the minted coin,
but the minted coin does not acquire the unminted coin.
Movable goods acquire the coin,
a coin does not acquire the movable goods.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same list and arrives at the basic case of goods versus money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking an אסימון acquires a minted coin, and taking goods acquires a coin; the reverse is not true in either case.

steps.title: The general rule: pulling the produce finalizes the sale, paying does not
steps.stepSummary: All goods traded for goods acquire each other. When buying produce, once the buyer pulls it the deal is final even if he has not paid. If he paid but did not pull it, either side can still back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: all movable goods acquire one another. How so? If he pulled produce from the seller and did not give him money, he cannot back out. If he gave him money and did not pull the produce, he can back out.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה sums up the list with a general rule and then shows how it works in a normal purchase of produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When goods are traded for goods, taking either item finalizes the whole deal. In a sale for money, the act that counts is pulling the goods (משיכה), not paying. So paid but not pulled means the deal is not yet final.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the general rule
He pulled; משיכה is the act of acquiring movable goods
Produce
To back out of the deal

steps.whatToRemember: For movable goods, the purchase becomes final through משיכה (pulling), not through paying. Money alone leaves the deal open.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume paying money completes the purchase. Here it is the opposite: the buyer can pay in full and the deal is still open until he pulls the produce.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כׇּל הַמִּטַּלְטְלִים קוֹנִין זֶה אֶת זֶה.
phrases.english: This is the rule: all movable goods acquire one another.
phrases.notes: In a trade of goods for goods, once one side takes his item, the other side owns the item he is getting.

phrases.english: How so? If he pulled produce from him
and did not give him money,
he cannot back out.
If he gave him money
and did not pull produce from him,
he can back out.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כׇּל הַמִּטַּלְטְלִים קוֹנִין זֶה אֶת זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the list of pairs with a general rule and a practical example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Goods traded for goods acquire each other. In a sale, pulling the produce finalizes it; paying money without pulling leaves it open to backing out.

steps.title: The curse of מי שפרע for someone who backs out
steps.stepSummary: Even where backing out is legally allowed, the חכמים warned that God, who punished the generations of the flood and of the tower, will punish whoever does not keep his word.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they said: The One who punished the people of the generation of the flood and the generation of the dispersion will punish whoever does not stand by his word.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a moral warning to the last case: money was paid, the goods were not yet pulled, and someone wants to back out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A court cannot stop him from backing out, because the deal is not legally final. Still, the חכמים said that God will hold him responsible for breaking his word. This is the curse known as מי שפרע.

keyTerms.meaning: But the חכמים said; adds a limit or warning to the rule
He who punished, meaning God; the name of this curse
The generation of the flood
The generation of the dispersion, at מגדל בבל
Stands by his word

steps.whatToRemember: Backing out after money was paid is legally possible, but it brings the curse of מי שפרע.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a deal can be open legally yet still be binding morally. Keeping your word matters even when a court cannot enforce it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אָמְרוּ: מִי שֶׁפָּרַע מֵאַנְשֵׁי דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
phrases.english: But they said: He who exacted payment from the people of the generation of the flood
phrases.notes: 'He who exacted payment' means God. 'They' are the חכמים.

phrases.english: and from the generation of the dispersion
phrases.notes: The people of מגדל בבל, who were scattered. See בראשית 11.

phrases.english: He will in the future exact payment
from whoever does not stand by his word.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל אָמְרוּ: מִי שֶׁפָּרַע מֵאַנְשֵׁי דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a moral warning to the 'paid but not pulled' case from the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who backs out after money was paid but before pulling the goods is under the curse of מי שפרע.

steps.title: רבי שמעון: The one holding the money has the upper hand
steps.stepSummary: The משנה closes with רבי שמעון's view that whoever has the money in his hand has the advantage when it comes to backing out of a deal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: Whoever has the money in his hand has the upper hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with a different opinion, from רבי שמעון. He says the person holding the money is in the stronger position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier part of the משנה said that if the buyer paid but did not pull the produce, either side may back out. רבי שמעון disagrees: only the side holding the money, the seller, may back out. The buyer, who already paid, cannot demand his money back.

keyTerms.meaning: His hand is on top: he has the advantage
Money (here meaning the payment)
In his hand

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה ends with two views on backing out of a deal: the ruling of the earlier part of the משנה, and רבי שמעון's view that the one holding the money has the upper hand.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
Whoever has the money in his hand
has the upper hand.
phrases.notes: He is talking about the earlier case where the buyer paid but didn't pull the produce yet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a dissenting view to the משנה's ruling on backing out of a sale.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The party holding the money has the upper hand.

steps.title: רבי teaches his son: Gold acquires silver
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with a story: רבי was teaching his son רבי שמעון the wording of our משנה, that taking gold acquires silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבי was teaching his son רבי שמעון: Gold acquires silver.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a story about רבי teaching the משנה's wording to his son. This sets up the son's question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording רבי teaches is exactly the opening of our משנה (step 17): when one side takes the gold, the other side acquires the silver. The story is told so that the son can point out a change in his father's teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
Was teaching (the wording of a משנה)
His son
Acquires

phrases.english: Gemara
Rabbi was teaching
phrases.notes: "רבי" with no name means רבי יהודה הנשיא, who put together the משנה.

phrases.english: to Rabbi Shimon, his son:
Gold acquires silver.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנֵי לֵיהּ רַבִּי לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא on the first line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking the gold acquires the silver.

steps.title: The son points out that his father once taught the opposite
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון reminds his father that when he was young he taught 'silver acquires gold', and now in his old age he teaches 'gold acquires silver'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: My teacher, in your youth you taught us 'silver acquires gold', and now in your old age you go back and teach us 'gold acquires silver'!
steps.whatsHappening: The son challenges his father's wording by pointing out that he used to teach the exact reverse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two versions are opposites. In the old version, taking silver acquires the gold. In the new version, taking gold acquires the silver. The son is not asking which is correct yet. He is pointing out that רבי changed his mind.

keyTerms.meaning: In your youth
In your old age
And you go back (change)
Gold

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. Youth: silver acquires gold. Old age: gold acquires silver, which is our משנה's wording.

phrases.english: He said to him: My teacher,
you taught us in your youth:
Silver acquires gold,
and now you go back and teach us in your old age:
Gold acquires silver!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי שָׁנִיתָ לָנוּ בְּיַלְדוּתֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording just taught by contrasting it with רבי's earlier version.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same teacher earlier taught the exact reverse ruling, so the change needs explaining.

steps.title: What was רבי's reasoning in each version?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי's thinking was when he was young, and what changed in his old age.
steps.simpleTranslation: In his youth, what did he hold? And in his old age, what did he hold?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind each of רבי's two versions. This sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story only told us that רבי changed his wording. Now the גמרא wants the logic behind each version: what made him think one way first and the other way later.

keyTerms.meaning: What did he hold? What was his reasoning?

phrases.english: In his youth, what did he hold,
and in his old age, what did he hold?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּיַלְדוּתֵיהּ מַאי סְבַר וּבְזִקְנוּתֵיהּ מַאי סָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the two versions the son contrasted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The logic behind each of רבי's two opposite versions.

steps.title: In his youth: Gold is currency, silver is goods
steps.stepSummary: When he was young, רבי held that gold, being more valuable, counts as the 'currency', and silver counts as the 'goods'. Taking goods acquires currency, so silver acquires gold.
steps.simpleTranslation: In his youth he held: gold, which is valuable, is currency. Silver, which is less valuable, is goods. And taking the goods acquires the currency.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי's first version: he treated gold as the money and silver as the item being bought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In any trade, one side is the 'payment' and the other is the 'item'. Pulling the item makes the deal final, as with goods acquiring coins in step 19. Since gold is worth more, young רבי saw it as the real money. That makes silver the item, so taking silver acquires the gold.

keyTerms.meaning: Currency: the coin used as payment
Literally 'fruit'; here the goods being bought
Valuable, important
Gold (Aramaic)
Silver (Aramaic)

steps.whyThisMatters: The whole debate depends on which coin counts as 'money' and which counts as 'goods'. That decides which side's taking makes the deal final.

phrases.english: In his youth he held:
Gold, which is valuable, is currency;
silver, which is not as valuable,
is goods,
and the goods acquire the currency.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּיַלְדוּתֵיהּ סְבַר דַּהֲבָא דַּחֲשִׁיב הָוֵי טִבְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of the question: the reasoning of רבי's youth.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In his youth, gold was considered currency and silver goods; taking goods acquires currency, so silver acquires gold.

steps.title: In his old age: Silver is the currency
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to explain רבי's later view, starting with silver. The explanation continues past this point.
steps.simpleTranslation: In his old age he held: silver...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts the second half of its answer: what רבי held in his old age. The sentence continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the later version says gold acquires silver, רבי must now see silver as the currency and gold as the goods. The reason he gives for this comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: In his old age

phrases.english: In his old age he held: silver...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the second half of the answer, the reasoning of רבי's old age.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In his old age רבי viewed silver as the currency (explanation continues).
